quests.instruction: Choose the clearest way to handle this.
quests.scene: A bank agent reads out a long reference number quickly over the phone and you missed the last few digits.
options: Could you say everything again from the very beginning, please?
Sorry, could you read the last four digits again, slowly?
Yes, got it, thanks. I'll work out the rest of it myself later.
Sorry, what was that? You're mumbling and the line is terrible.
quests.hint: Ask for only the piece you missed.
quests.explanation: Naming exactly which part you missed makes repeating quick and easy. Asking for everything again wastes time, blaming the agent is unfair, and pretending you got it defeats the purpose of the call.
quests.culturalNote: Asking for a repeat of a specific part is normal in phone calls, especially with numbers.

quests.instruction: Pick the response that fits the situation.
quests.scene: Your manager asks you to 'make the poster pop' but doesn't explain what she means.
options: Sure, I'll take care of it and let you know when it's ready.
When you say 'pop', do you mean brighter colors or a bolder layout?
I'm afraid I don't really understand design terms, sorry about that.
Could you just tell me exactly what needs changing on it?
quests.hint: Offer two concrete interpretations to help her pick.
quests.explanation: Giving options makes it easy for her to explain what she wants. Agreeing blindly risks a wasted revision, and the other replies push the work back onto her.
quests.culturalNote: Vague creative feedback is common; offering options turns it into a quick decision.

quests.scene: Your teacher says, 'Read pages twenty to thirty for Monday.' You're not sure whether page thirty counts.
options: Are we supposed to read all of it or just skim through it?
Is that a lot of reading for one weekend, do you think?
I'll read as much of it as I possibly can before Monday.
Just to check, is page thirty included?
quests.hint: Ask only about the detail that is unclear.
quests.explanation: A short targeted question resolves the doubt. Asking about depth, workload, or promising effort doesn't answer whether the last page is included.
quests.culturalNote: Ranges like 'twenty to thirty' are often ambiguous about the final number.

quests.scene: A friend said 'seven-fifteen' but you heard 'seven-fifty' and arrived late to the cinema.
options: Oh no, I thought you said seven-fifty — I must have misheard. Sorry!
You definitely said seven-fifty, I'm sure I remember it clearly.
Well, you should have texted me the exact time to make sure.
It's only a few minutes, and the trailers are still playing, right?
quests.hint: Own your side of the mix-up without turning it into a blame game.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging what you misheard and apologizing lets the moment pass. Insisting you're right or blaming her escalates a small mistake.
quests.culturalNote: Times like fifteen and fifty sound alike, especially in noisy places.

quests.scene: A colleague read your email as approval, but you actually meant you needed more details before deciding.
options: I think my email was unclear — I meant I need more details before I can approve it.
I think you may have misread my email, since I never said yes.
I never said I would approve it, so please check what I wrote.
Let's forget the email. I'll just approve it now to keep things moving, and we can sort out the details later.
quests.hint: Take responsibility for the wording without giving in.
quests.explanation: Owning the unclear wording while restating your position resolves it without blame. Accusing him or approving anyway leaves the real issue unsolved.
quests.culturalNote: In written communication, ambiguity is often shared; acknowledging your part helps.

quests.scene: You called about a refund, but the agent keeps explaining how to exchange the item.
options: No, that isn't what I asked. Are you actually listening to me?
I think there's a misunderstanding — I'm asking about a refund, not an exchange.
An exchange is fine, I suppose, if that's all that you can offer me today, though it isn't what I wanted.
Could I speak to someone else who might understand my problem?
quests.hint: State what you want, calmly, and name the mismatch.
quests.explanation: Naming the gap and your actual request corrects the direction without accusing anyone. Snapping or settling for the wrong outcome doesn't solve anything.
quests.culturalNote: Misunderstandings in service calls are common; a calm restatement usually works best.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: A close friend says 'I'm fine' but has been unusually quiet all evening.
options: I know you're not fine, so you might as well tell me.
Okay, if you say so. I'll leave you alone about it, then.
Is this about what happened with Sam yesterday, by any chance?
You seem a bit quiet — are you sure you're okay?
quests.hint: Show you noticed and leave room for an honest answer.
quests.explanation: A gentle check-in shows you noticed without forcing an answer. Pressing or guessing the cause puts him on the defensive.
quests.culturalNote: Between friends, one gentle follow-up is usually welcome after 'I'm fine'.

quests.scene: You invited a friend for coffee and she replied only with 'K.' Her earlier texts were warm and chatty.
options: Why are you being so rude? I only asked if you wanted coffee.
Your reply felt a bit short — is everything okay, or is the plan not working?
Great, see you there then, and I'll grab us a table by the window.
Did I say something wrong? I really can't tell what's happening.
quests.hint: Name what you noticed, and offer an easy way out.
quests.explanation: Describing the change and offering two options makes it easy to answer honestly. Accusations or ignoring it leave the uncertainty in place.
quests.culturalNote: Text messages lose tone, so a short check is better than assuming.

quests.scene: A colleague says, 'We should catch up sometime.' You'd like to, and you're not sure she means it.
options: Sure, sometime. That sounds really nice, let's keep in touch.
Do you actually mean it, or are you just being polite?
You always say that, and then we never actually do it.
I'd like that — how about coffee on Thursday?
quests.hint: Turn a vague line into a concrete plan.
quests.explanation: Suggesting a specific time tests the invitation kindly and makes it real. Vague agreement or challenge make it awkward.
quests.culturalNote: Phrases like 'catch up sometime' are often courtesy; a concrete offer shows what you really want.

quests.scene: A courier left a parcel addressed to your neighbor Ravi in your hallway by mistake.
options: Hi, I think a parcel meant for you was delivered to me by mistake — shall I drop it over?
I've got your parcel here, so come and pick it up when you can.
Your parcel is at my place. The couriers around here are useless, they dump things at the wrong door every single week.
Is your name Ravi? A parcel arrived at my door earlier today.
quests.hint: Explain what happened and offer to fix it.
quests.explanation: Explaining the mix-up and offering to bring it over is clear and neighborly. The others push the effort onto him or lead with complaints.
quests.culturalNote: Misdelivered parcels are common; a friendly note usually resolves them quickly.

quests.scene: In a shop, a customer mistakes you for an employee and asks where the umbrellas are.
options: Do I look like I work here to you? I'm just shopping like you.
No, I'm just a customer, so I really can't help you with that.
No. Ask someone wearing the uniform, they'll know where they are.
Sorry, I don't work here — but the staff are by the entrance.
quests.hint: Clear up the mistake and still point her somewhere useful.
quests.explanation: Correcting the mistake and directing her helps without offense. Defensive or curt replies turn an innocent error into friction.
quests.culturalNote: Being mistaken for staff is common; a kind redirect is the easiest response.

quests.scene: In a meeting, your manager assigns you to the Atlas project, but you're actually on the Beacon project.
options: That's Priya's project, not mine, so I think you meant her.
No, you've got that wrong, and it's not the first time either.
Just to clarify, I'm on the Beacon project — Priya is on Atlas.
I think you must mean someone else, because that isn't me.
quests.hint: State the correct information plainly and without blame.
quests.explanation: Clarifying facts calmly, without judging her memory, keeps the meeting on track. Contradiction or sarcasm makes her look bad publicly.
quests.culturalNote: Correcting a manager works better as clarification than as contradiction.

quests.scene: You gave a tourist directions and realize a minute later you sent him the wrong way. You catch up with him.
options: Actually, I'm not sure about it. Just try that way and see.
Sorry, I sent you the wrong way — it's the other street, past the bakery.
You should have asked someone else who knew the area better, because I only moved here recently.
Did you go left? Turn around and go the other way instead.
quests.hint: Own your mistake and give the corrected route.
quests.explanation: Admitting the error and giving the fix is honest and useful. Vague, blaming, or unclear replies leave him lost.
quests.culturalNote: Correcting your own mistake quickly is usually appreciated, even by strangers.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: You posted the wrong meeting time (3 p.m. instead of 4 p.m.) in the team chat and someone has already replied 'see you at 3'.
options: Meeting time changed. New time is 4, so please note that.
Correction: the meeting is at 4, not 3. Sorry for the mix-up!
Ignore my last message and just check the calendar invite.
Sorry, some of you might have got the wrong time from me.
quests.hint: Say what was wrong and what's right, in the same message.
quests.explanation: Stating both the error and the fix leaves no confusion. Vague messages or pointing to elsewhere make people work it out.
quests.culturalNote: In team chats, corrections should be explicit and in the same thread.

quests.scene: Halfway through an interview, you realize you gave the wrong year for when you left your last job.
options: I should correct something I said earlier — I left that company in 2019, not 2020.
Sorry, I think I said the wrong date earlier, but never mind that.
The exact dates don't matter too much, do they, as long as it's roughly right?
I'll double-check my dates and email you the exact answer afterwards.
quests.hint: Fix the mistake right away and be specific.
quests.explanation: Correcting immediately with the accurate date shows honesty. Brushing it off or delaying looks careless.
quests.culturalNote: Interviewers usually respect candidates who correct themselves promptly.

quests.scene: You made a sarcastic joke and your friend looks hurt, as if you meant it.
options: I was only joking — I'm sorry it came across that way.
You're way too sensitive about things like this.
It was just a joke, relax, nobody else is offended.
I didn't mean anything by it, so there's nothing to be upset about.
quests.hint: Take responsibility for the impact, not just the intent.
quests.explanation: Apologizing for how it landed acknowledges her feelings. Blaming her sensitivity or denying meaning invalidates them.
quests.culturalNote: Humor depends on shared context; owning the impact repairs trust.

quests.scene: A coworker says you ignored his email from yesterday, but you never received it.
options: I never got it, so you must have sent it to the wrong address.
I'm sure I replied to it already, so check your sent folder.
I don't see it in my inbox — could you resend it? Maybe it went to spam.
Just tell me what it said, since email is so unreliable anyway and I've missed messages from other people too.
quests.hint: State what you see and suggest a fix.
quests.explanation: Saying what you see and offering a fix keeps it factual. Blaming or bluffing leaves the issue unresolved.
quests.culturalNote: Email delivery problems are common and rarely anyone's fault.

quests.scene: A neighbor complains about your dog barking last night, but your dog was indoors all evening.
options: It's not my dog, so I really don't see why you're complaining to me about it at this hour of the day.
My dog doesn't bark, so you must be mistaken about that.
Well, I'll try to keep him quieter from now on, sorry.
I don't think it was mine — my dog was inside all evening. Could it be next door's?
quests.hint: Politely give facts without accepting blame for something you didn't do.
quests.explanation: Sharing facts calmly and suggesting another source keeps it neighborly. Denial or blindly accepting blame both cause trouble.
quests.culturalNote: Barking complaints often need a bit of detective work; facts help.

quests.scene: Your restaurant bill includes a dessert you didn't order.
options: You've overcharged me, and I'd like this fixed right away.
This bill is wrong, so please sort it out for me quickly.
I think there's a mistake — I didn't order the dessert. Could you check?
I'll pay it, but it isn't right and I'm not happy about it.
quests.hint: Point out the error politely and ask for a check.
quests.explanation: Politely naming the item and asking for a check makes fixing easy. Accusing or grudgingly paying doesn't fix the mistake.
quests.culturalNote: Bill errors are usually accidental; calm requests get them fixed fastest.

quests.scene: A hotel says your booking is for the 12th, but you meant the 21st and realize you typed the date wrong.
options: I think I entered the wrong date when I booked — I meant the 21st. Is there any way to change it?
Your website is really confusing and the calendar is badly designed. I clearly meant the 21st, so it's your problem to fix.
I booked the 21st, whatever your system says on the screen.
Could I just take a room for the 12th instead of the 21st?
quests.hint: Admit the mistake and ask about options.
quests.explanation: Owning the error and asking what's possible invites help. Blaming the site or insisting doesn't help the staff help you.
quests.culturalNote: Hotels can often help if you own the mistake quickly.

quests.instruction: Choose the clearest way to handle this.
quests.scene: A receptionist misspells your surname while checking you in for a medical appointment.
options: It's Olu something, it's already written on the form there.
You'll find it if you look at my appointment card properly.
Let me spell that for you: O-L-U-W-A-S-E-Y-I.
It's a long name, so just use my first name instead.
quests.hint: Give the receptionist what she needs to get it right.
quests.explanation: Spelling it out lets her record it correctly. Vague or dismissive replies risk errors in your medical record.
quests.culturalNote: Names can be hard to spell; spelling them aloud is normal and appreciated.

quests.scene: In a group chat, you wrote 'great, another meeting' and a colleague replied: 'Wow, sorry you feel that way.' You actually like the idea.
options: Why would you think I was being sarcastic? That's a strange reading.
Never mind, just ignore my message and carry on with the plan.
To be clear, I wasn't being sarcastic — I do like the idea.
Some people read way too much into a short text message.
quests.hint: Say plainly what you meant.
quests.explanation: A direct statement clears the tone up. Blaming his reading or retreating leaves the confusion.
quests.culturalNote: Written sarcasm is often missed; plain clarification is best.

quests.scene: A stranger on a bench asks, 'Do you mind if I sit here?' You're happy for her to sit.
options: Yes, go ahead. I'll move my bag over a bit for you.
Not at all — please, sit.
Yes please do, I've been waiting for someone to join me.
I don't mind. Sit, sit, but try not to talk too much.
quests.hint: 'Do you mind' asks about a problem, so think about what 'yes' means.
quests.explanation: 'Not at all' correctly says no problem to 'Do you mind'. A plain 'yes' can sound like refusal, and the others are confusing or oddly phrased.
quests.culturalNote: Answering 'Do you mind?' with 'Yes' can be read as 'I do mind', so 'Not at all' is safest.

quests.scene: Your manager says, 'You might want to reconsider that approach.' You're not sure whether it's advice or an instruction.
options: Okay, I'll keep it as it is and see how it turns out. If it doesn't work, we can always discuss it again next week.
So you're saying it's wrong, is that what you mean?
Would you like me to change it? I want to make sure I understand what you'd prefer.
I've thought about it and I still disagree with you.
quests.hint: Check what she wants without sounding defensive.
quests.explanation: Asking what she prefers clarifies the meaning without pushback. Defensive or dismissive replies can turn a suggestion into a conflict.
quests.culturalNote: Indirect language from managers can be advice or instruction; asking removes doubt.

quests.scene: Your roommate says, 'Can you do the dishes?' It's unclear whether she wants them done now or later tonight.
options: I'll do them at some point, just give me a little while.
Why is it always me who has to do them in this house?
Right now? I'm in the middle of something, so maybe later.
Sure — do you need them done now, or is tonight fine?
quests.hint: Say yes and ask about timing.
quests.explanation: Agreeing and checking timing settles the request quickly. Vague promises or complaints leave it unresolved.
quests.culturalNote: Requests often leave timing unspoken; asking is quicker than guessing.

quests.scene: A client emails: 'Please send the report ASAP.' You could send it by end of day or in an hour.
options: When you say ASAP, would end of today work, or do you need it sooner?
I'll do my best to send it to you as soon as possible.
ASAP isn't really possible, so please give me a real deadline, because I have several other clients waiting on me today too.
I'll send it as soon as I can get to it this afternoon.
quests.hint: Turn 'ASAP' into an actual time.
quests.explanation: Offering a concrete option makes the deadline clear. Vague reassurance or pushback leaves it undefined.
quests.culturalNote: 'ASAP' means different things to different people; a specific time avoids disappointment.

quests.scene: A friend texts, 'Let's meet near the station.' The station has a main entrance and a separate bus stop area.
options: Near which station do you mean? There are several in town.
I'll find you, don't worry, just send me a message later.
Text me when you're there and I'll come over to you.
Which side of the station — the main entrance or the bus stops?
quests.hint: Ask about the detail that could send you to the wrong place.
quests.explanation: A specific question removes the real ambiguity. Asking things you already know or leaving it open risks missing each other.
quests.culturalNote: 'Near' is vague at big stations; agreeing on an exact spot saves stress.

quests.scene: You and a colleague cleared up a misunderstanding that had made her upset for two days.
options: See, it was a misunderstanding, so it wasn't really my fault.
Fine, but you should have told me sooner that you were upset.
I'm glad we sorted that out — I should have asked earlier.
It's okay now, so let's just forget it ever happened.
quests.hint: Reconnect and share responsibility for the delay.
quests.explanation: Acknowledging your own part rebuilds trust. Blaming or dismissing hurts the repair.
quests.culturalNote: Sharing responsibility for a misunderstanding helps restore the relationship.

quests.scene: At a noisy market, a vendor says a price you think was 'twelve euros', but it might have been 'two-ten'.
options: Twelve euros? That's really expensive for something so small.
Fine, I'll take it and count my change when I get home.
Just to confirm — that's twelve euros in total?
Could I pay a lower price if I take two of them?
quests.hint: Confirm the number you think you heard.
quests.explanation: Repeating the price checks your understanding. Reacting or moving on could lead to paying the wrong amount.
quests.culturalNote: Confirming numbers aloud is standard where noise or accents may cause mishearing.

quests.scene: At the end of a meeting, you and your colleague agreed some tasks but the details were a little loose.
options: Great, so we're all clear then and can go on with our work.
I'll take care of everything myself and keep you updated later on, so you don't need to worry about any of it whatsoever.
Could you send notes after this meeting, so we're all sure?
Let me make sure I've got this right: I'll send the draft Friday and you'll review it Monday.
quests.hint: Summarize agreements in specific terms.
quests.explanation: A specific summary checks shared understanding and creates a record. General agreement leaves room for confusion.
quests.culturalNote: Restating agreements is a common professional way to prevent misunderstandings.
